answers.answer: An HTTP cache stores response bodies and metadata (status/headers) for reuse. A browser private cache serves its user agent; a CDN is shared caches at edge servers near users; origin is responsible for the resource. A hit reuses a suitable response; a miss has none usable. Empty: GET browser → CDN → origin, response origin → CDN → browser, with storage only where policy permits. A browser hit avoids network; another browser missing locally can hit the CDN and avoid origin. Stored objects are responses, not replicated database records; origin may consult a database, but hits need not reach either. CDN request hit ratio is hits/requests at that layer: 800/1000 = 80%; the 200 other requests produce exactly 200 origin requests under the stated assumptions. Browser hits never reach that denominator; varying response sizes prevent deriving byte savings, and real validation, refresh, additional layers and application/database work need separate measurement. Repeated public assets can improve nearby-response latency and reduce origin requests/transfer. CDN requests/transfer incur potential charges plus key configuration, invalidation and monitoring costs. Omit shared caching for low-traffic, mostly private or rarely reused Notes responses when measured reuse, latency and total-cost benefits do not justify it; preserve privacy policies.

evidence.quote: An HTTP cache stores response bodies and metadata, such as status and headers, for reuse.
With empty caches, the request goes browser → CDN → origin. The response returns origin → CDN → browser, with storage at each cache only if its policy permits.
A browser hit avoids the network request. After a browser miss, a CDN hit avoids origin.
The ratio is 800 / 1,000 = 80%. If each other request makes exactly one origin request, with no extra layers or background requests, origin receives 200.
Browser hits never entered that denominator. Request hit ratio is not byte hit ratio: response sizes differ.
CDN requests and transfer can incur charges; key configuration, invalidation and monitoring add operational work.
For a low-traffic application serving mostly private or rarely reused responses, omit shared caching if measured benefits do not justify those costs.

answers.answer: Cache-Control supplies response caching directives. public permits shared caching subject to other rules; max-age=60 sets a 60-second freshness lifetime; s-maxage=300 overrides that only for shared caches. Fresh means policy permits reuse without validation; stale means the freshness limit was reached, without requiring body deletion. Age estimates seconds since origin generation or successful validation, including cache time. At Age 90 the browser is stale by 30 seconds (60−90=−30; zero fresh seconds remain), while the CDN is fresh with 300−90=210 seconds left. Delivery neither resets age nor proves the origin unchanged. A representation is the returned resource form; revalidation checks stored-representation usability. ETag is an opaque representation validator, preserved as supplied. The stale CDN sends conditional GET with If-None-Match: "v1", requesting a body only if the selected representation no longer matches. Unchanged: origin returns 304 without replacement body; CDN updates applicable metadata including freshness and serves its retained v1 body for the ordinary browser GET. Changed: origin returns 200 with new v2 body and ETag: "v2"; CDN answers with the new body and replaces the stored representation if policy allows. ETag does not push updates elsewhere. Validation contacts origin; 304 saves body transfer on that hop, not the round trip or necessarily application/database work.

evidence.quote: s-maxage overrides it only in shared caches; the browser still uses 60 seconds.
Age estimates seconds since generation or successful validation at origin, including time spent through caches.

If this response arrives with Age: 90, ignoring transit and clock differences, the browser is 30 seconds past its lifetime. The CDN has 300 − 90 = 210 seconds of freshness left. Receiving it does not start a new full lifetime.
Freshness is permission to reuse, not proof that origin content is unchanged.

A representation is the returned form of a resource, such as a page's HTML. Revalidation checks whether the stored representation remains usable. ETag is an opaque validator identifying that representation; clients preserve the tag rather than interpreting it.
It sends a conditional GET to origin with If-None-Match: "v1", asking for the body only if the selected representation no longer matches.

If unchanged, origin returns 304 Not Modified without a replacement body. The CDN updates applicable stored metadata, including freshness information, and uses its retained body to answer the browser's ordinary GET.
If changed, origin returns 200 with the new body and its validator, for example ETag: "v2".
Origin was still contacted and may run application logic or query a database to decide whether the representation changed.

answers.answer: Cookies are browser-held state; Set-Cookie asks the browser to store it and Cookie sends it back. Authorization is a credential-carrying request header. Authentication establishes identity; authorization checks resource permission. Choose Cache-Control: no-cache for the public page: storage allowed, successful validation required before every reuse. Choose Cache-Control: private for the private note: shared storage forbidden, browser storage allowed, other directives still apply; private alone does not require validation each use. Choose Cache-Control: no-store for the sensitive note: HTTP caches must not store it. This cannot erase earlier copies or replace permission checks. Cookie/Set-Cookie neither automatically partition entries by user nor universally prevent caching. Authorization-bearing requests have special shared-cache restrictions, but response policy can permit reuse; authentication alone does not guarantee CDN bypass. Reusing one user’s response for another can expose private data. Keep origin authorization, explicitly configure private/no-store as appropriate, verify actual CDN rules prevent shared storage and reuse, and test different users. Do not make personalized responses public to improve hit rates.

evidence.quote: Cookies are browser-held state: Set-Cookie asks the browser to store it; Cookie sends it back. Authorization is a request header carrying credentials. Authentication establishes identity; authorization checks permission to access a resource.
For a public page, unqualified no-cache allows storage but requires successful validation before every reuse.

For a private response where browser storage is acceptable, private forbids shared-cache storage; it neither forbids browser storage nor requires validation on every use. Other directives still apply.
For a sensitive response, no-store instructs HTTP caches not to store the response. It cannot erase previously delivered copies or replace permission checks.
Cookie and Set-Cookie do not automatically create per-user cache entries or universally prevent caching.
Authorization-bearing requests have special shared-cache restrictions, but response policy can permit reuse; authentication alone is no universal CDN bypass guarantee.

Keep authorization at origin. For private routes, verify that explicit private/no-store policies and actual CDN rules prevent shared storage and reuse. Test different users; do not mark personalized responses public for a higher hit rate.

answers.answer: A cache key identifies the stored response that can satisfy a request; variants are different returned forms of a resource. HTTP caching matches method/target URL and selected request headers. Preserve pdf versus html format query values and en versus fr language values. Vary identifies a request header whose value must match for reuse: Vary: Accept-Language separates language variants when supported and honored. If the CDN ignores query parameters, verify and correct actual matching settings so both format and language survive, or bypass caching until they do. Dropping format can serve HTML to a PDF request; dropping language can mix language variants. Irrelevant tracking parameters multiply entries and reduce hits; remove them only after confirming response content is unaffected. Vary neither changes the URL nor grants permission nor overrides private/no-store; it does not authorize sharing private notes.

evidence.quote: A cache key identifies which stored response can satisfy a request. HTTP caching uses the method and target URL, with selected request headers distinguishing variants: different returned forms of the same resource.

Keep the format query values distinct. A CDN configured to ignore them could return HTML for a PDF request; verify the actual key settings rather than assuming every CDN includes every query parameter.
Vary: Accept-Language tells a cache that this request header's value must match for reuse.
CDN support and custom keys differ: verify that both format and language survive the actual matching rules, or bypass caching until they do.
Irrelevant tracking parameters can create extra entries and fewer hits. Exclude them only after confirming they do not change the response.
Vary does not change the URL, grant permission or override private/no-store.

answers.answer: A versioned asset URL changes when the bytes change. Publish changed JavaScript at app.v2.js, keeping each version URL immutable so long caching fits; update the referring page to request v2. An old cached referring page may still request v1. A mutable page keeping its URL needs freshness/revalidation chosen for tolerated update delay, such as short freshness or validation on every reuse. Database edits do not rewrite stored HTTP responses. A CDN purge removes or invalidates targeted CDN entries under provider behavior; verify relevant URLs, variants, CDN cache layers, propagation and completion. Purge is not simultaneous replacement everywhere and does not evict fresh browser copies or erase downloaded content. Unpublishing can stop future origin access and trigger purges, but cannot instantly revoke already delivered public content; choose lifetimes with that constraint. No provider-specific purge procedure or numeric completion guarantee is supplied.

evidence.quote: A versioned asset URL changes when its bytes change: publish app.v2.js instead of overwriting app.v1.js.
Update the referring page to request v2; an old cached page can still ask for v1.
A mutable page that keeps its URL needs a chosen freshness/revalidation policy matching the tolerated update delay. A database edit does not rewrite stored HTTP responses.
A CDN purge removes or invalidates targeted CDN entries according to the provider. Verify coverage of the relevant URLs, variants and CDN cache layers, plus propagation and completion behavior.

Purging CDN entries does not evict fresh browser copies or erase downloaded content. Unpublishing can stop future origin access and trigger purges, but already delivered public content cannot be instantly revoked.

answers.answer: stale-while-revalidate permits bounded stale reuse while attempting background validation, hiding validation latency; stale-if-error permits bounded fallback on eligible errors. These are optional permissions, not freshness or availability guarantees. Freshness lasts 60 seconds; allowances start at expiry. At age 75 the copy is 15 seconds stale, within the additional 30-second window ending at age 90: it may be served while background validation is attempted. At age 150 an eligible error permits reuse because it is 90 seconds stale, within the additional 120-second error window ending at age 180. At age 200 it is 140 seconds stale and neither directive authorizes stale reuse. A cold cache has no fallback; exhausted windows can expose failure. Support and policy must be verified. These permissions do not override private/no-store; private-data correctness or urgent removal may prohibit serving stale copies despite availability benefits.

evidence.quote: stale-while-revalidate permits bounded stale reuse while attempting background validation, hiding validation latency. stale-if-error permits bounded stale fallback on eligible errors, such as an origin failure.
These are optional permissions, not freshness or availability promises.

At age 75 it is 15 seconds stale: the additional 30-second background-validation window permits reuse while refreshing, through age 90. At age 150 with an eligible error, it is 90 seconds stale: the error allowance lasts another 120 seconds after expiry, through age 180. At age 200 neither extension still permits stale reuse.
A cold cache has no response to fall back to, and exhausted allowances can expose the failure.

Verify provider support and policy; these directives do not override private/no-store. Private-data correctness or urgent removal may forbid stale reuse even when it improves public-help availability.
